summary:
Colorado's own law prohibits discrimination on the basis of gender identity or expression in employment, housing, public accommodations, education and credit, a coverage that dates to 2008 and was expanded again in 2025 through the Colorado Anti-Discrimination Act. The Kelly Loving Act, signed by Governor Jared Polis on 16 May 2025, requires employers and schools to use a person's chosen name and pronouns, bars deadnaming and misgendering, requires schools with dress codes to allow any uniform option, and simplifies gender-marker changes on birth certificates and driver's licences from 1 October 2026. As of 12 October 2026, the state's gender-identity policy score stood at 23.25 out of 25 in the Movement Advancement Project's equality mapping.

Identity documents are comparatively open. The surgical requirement for changing the gender marker on a birth certificate was removed unanimously by the Board of Public Health and Environment in February 2019; a Change of Sex Designation form suffices for licences and IDs through the Division of Motor Vehicles, and Birth Certificate Correction and Sex Designation forms go to the Department of Public Health and Environment. Birth certificates offer M, F and X markers, and IDs and licences offer male, female and X. Minors need parent or guardian consent plus a medical or mental health professional's involvement.

Hate-crime law has covered gender identity or expression since 2001 with penalty enhancements for bias-motivated crimes. In 2009 a Greeley jury convicted a man of first-degree murder with a hate-crime finding in what was described as the first murder trial applying a hate-crime law where the victim was transgender. The anti-bullying statute also prohibits bullying on the basis of gender identity and requires school districts to adopt prevention policies.

Facilities access is protected. In 2013 the Colorado Civil Rights Division ruled that transgender six-year-old Coy Mathis could use the girls' bathroom at her elementary school in Fountain, and in 2023 Colorado implemented a law granting full access to bathroom facilities for all genders. There is no state bathroom ban of the kind in force in nine states and one territory.

Care access is contested on two fronts. The Colorado Supreme Court ruled 5-2 on 18 May 2026 that Children's Hospital Colorado violated state anti-discrimination law by suspending gender-affirming care for transgender youth under federal pressure, ordering an injunction requiring the hospital to resume puberty blockers and hormone therapy; Justice William Hood wrote that continuing such treatment for cisgender children while stopping it for transgender youth meant the decision denied petitioners the full and equal enjoyment of services based on gender identity, and two justices dissented citing federal threats to the hospital system. Separately, Colorado will suspend Medicaid coverage for hormone therapy, puberty blockers and other gender-affirming care for transgender youth beginning 13 October 2026 because a federal rule finalised in August 2026 blocks federal funds for such care under 18 (and under 19 under the CHP+ child programme); about 500 youth under 19 received Medicaid-covered hormone therapy for gender dysphoria in fiscal 2024-25, patients already on hormones keep coverage through a six-month tapering period, behavioural healthcare is unaffected, and the state Medicaid agency said resuming coverage will require legislative action.

Insurance coverage is comparatively broad. Basic health insurance in Colorado must explicitly include sexual reassignment surgery as a basic policy from 2023, and a July 2026 national assessment counts Colorado among the states with comprehensive health-insurance laws covering facial-hair removal and expanded gender-related coverage. The same assessment lists Colorado among the most protective states for transgender people.

Conversion therapy on minors was banned statewide by a bill signed 31 May 2019. Following the U.S. Supreme Court's 31 March 2026 ruling in Chiles v. Salazar by 8-1 requiring strict scrutiny of that ban, Colorado passed HB 26-1322 on 8 May 2026, which redefines conversion therapy as direction toward a pre-determined gender identity or sexual orientation outcome and removes the statute of limitations for claims.

Prison conditions are governed by litigation rather than statute. A 2019 class action on behalf of transgender women held in men's prisons alleged the Colorado Department of Corrections subjected them to sexual and physical violence and denied medically necessary care. A court-approved 2024 consent decree in Denver District Court (Raven v. Polis) required the department to expand health care, create voluntary specialised housing (a 100-bed unit at the men's Sterling facility and an integration unit at the women's prison), and pay about $2.1 million to roughly 400 class members without admitting liability. A 2019 settlement (Lindsay Saunders-Velez, $170,000) addressed the safety of a transgender inmate held in a men's prison. No identity-based-housing statute governs placement; trans women were historically held in men's prisons, with relief achieved through litigation and consent decree rather than a baseline housing rule.

State-level school sports policy is moving in the opposite direction. In April 2025 the D49 school board voted 3-2 to advance a policy banning biologically male students from female sports and vice versa, the D-11 Board voted 6-1 in June 2025 for a similar policy with Academy District 20 following suit, and in December 2025 an undisclosed lawsuit settlement was reached over banning trans individuals from playing on female sports teams within some association governing districts. Colorado voters will decide in November 2026 whether to ban transgender kids from gendered sports that do not align with their biological sex (Initiative 109) and to prohibit surgery on a child for the purpose of altering their sex characteristics (Initiative 110), after state elections officials certified voter signatures on three measures including Initiative 108 on child sex trafficking; the initiatives were pushed by conservative activists and would, if passed, write restrictions on transgender minors into state law.

Colorado also protects safe passage: April 2023 legislation was signed to protect, defend and guarantee gender-affirming healthcare services and the safe passage of transgender individuals from interstate travel.
tangentialFactors:
Colorado's protections operate under direct federal-funding pressure. The Medicaid suspension beginning 13 October 2026 shows that state-level guarantees can be overridden where federal money is involved, and the state Medicaid agency has said resuming coverage will require legislative action. A visitor who relies on Medicaid or a federally funded programme should not assume Colorado's statutory protections will hold.

The Children's Hospital Colorado ruling demonstrates that federal pressure has already caused at least one major provider to suspend care, even though the state Supreme Court ordered it reinstated. Two justices dissented on the ground that federal threats could shut the hospital system, so the durability of the injunction is not settled.

Colorado is one of nine states listed in a July 2026 assessment as most protective for transgender people, alongside California, Connecticut, Hawaii, Illinois, Massachusetts, Maryland, Minnesota and New Jersey. That ranking is a policy-score comparison, not a measure of incident rates.

Ballot initiatives in November 2026 could restrict transgender minors in sports and in medical care. Until the vote, the current state of the law is Colorado's protective framework; after the vote, the position may change, and a visitor travelling with a trans minor should check the outcome.

School-district policies in Colorado Springs-area districts (D49, D-11, Academy District 20) already restrict trans students' participation in school sports independent of state statute, and a December 2025 lawsuit settlement addressed bans in some association governing districts. Enforcement of sports restrictions therefore varies by district and by athletic association rather than following a single statewide rule.

Colorado's hate-crime conviction in 2009 and the 2013 Coy Mathis ruling are individual data points illustrating how the state's protections have been applied; they do not establish a general level of safety for trans visitors.

outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the November 2026 ballot initiatives (109 and 110) will pass is unresolved; they are certified for the ballot but not yet decided.

The terms of the December 2025 lawsuit settlement over trans participation in female sports teams within some association governing districts are undisclosed in the source and cannot be stated.

The scope and duration of the injunction ordering Children's Hospital Colorado to resume gender-affirming care, and whether federal pressure will produce further litigation, are unresolved.

Whether the Colorado Legislature will act to restore Medicaid coverage of gender-affirming care after 13 October 2026 is unresolved; the state Medicaid agency has said legislative action is required but no bill is identified in the sources.

No region-specific incident data on violence against trans visitors in Colorado is provided in the inventory; the 2009 Greeley hate-crime murder conviction and the 2022 Colorado Springs gay-bar shooting (which targeted sexual orientation rather than gender identity) are the only bias-crime data points, and neither establishes a current rate.

The source inventory does not address how Colorado's document rules interact with federal passport processing under Executive Order 14168; a state-issued X marker does not guarantee a federal passport will carry one.
